newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa off highs by close, still buoyant.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa off highs by close, still buoyant.

text.p: LIFFE cocoa futures ended Tuesday at one-year highs on aggressive fund and spec buying on the back of a bullish chart picture.
Benchmark September gained 11 stg to end at 1,141 stg a tonne, the best finish since June 1996. But prices were off intraday the high of 1,162 on late profit-taking.
New York's inability to extend its steep gains on Monday also contributed to some liquidation in London.
But the overall technical outlook remains buoyant. Traders said while there could be some correction to an overbought condition, the mood remained upbeat.
"It's a very good move on the upside and the charts remained constructive," said one trader.
Another said: "It is being stoked up by spec buying. Fundamentally, there's no particular reason to be bullish, nothing has changed."

In one latest fundamental development, weather analysts said heavy mid-June rains in Ivory Coast raised wet season rainfall totals to at least average levels and boosted prospects for the 1997/98 (Oct-April) main cocoa crop.
Fund buying chased New York cocoa futures to new eight-year peaks on Monday amid bullish technical indicators.
Volume was brisk with a hefty 17,153 lots changing hands, led by forward September and December. By the close, December stood 20 higher at 1,150 to command a three stg premium to September.
Cocoa has risen by 15 percent since early June on the back of bullish chart picture and concerns over longer-term weather-related supply situation.
There had been worries that the developing El Nino weather pattern and the current crop development in West Africa could affect the coming 1997/98 crop.
Some traders said it was still too early to say that there would be a crop shortage next season.
This week's rally was fuelled by a smaller-than-expected rise in net speculative long positions as of June 17 in New York.

The U.S. CFTC Commitment of Traders report, released late on Friday, showed speculators were net long some 25,000 lots, which was below most traders' expectations of a 30,000-lot speculative net long position.
"In August 1994, the net longs were 41,000 tonnes. Based on the current 25,000 lots, there's an awful lot of buying to be done," said one.
